item.title: Contrary to popular perception, most people will not adopt a new technology just because it makes them more efficient. Instead, they’ll adopt new technology because: - Someone they know who’s similar to them on some dimension adopted the technology, and got positive results (eg became cooler, riche...
item.description:
作者：Zara Zhang 账号：@zarazhangrui 简介：Builder. Dangerously skips permissions. Harvard’17. GitHub: https://t.co/KCuEajezlL YouTube: https://t.co/8xzbGWtf6w
Contrary to popular perception, most people will not adopt a new technology just because it makes them more efficient.
Instead, they’ll adopt new technology because: - Someone they know who’s similar to them on some dimension adopted the technology, and got positive results (eg became cooler, richer, more popular/respected), and they wanna become like that person - They feel like everyone around them has adopted the technology, and if they don’t, they’ll be left behind
Notice that it’s not entirely a rational decision. It’s more of an EMOTIONAL decision.
So if you’re trying to make someone adopt a new technology, the messaging shouldn’t be “this will make you 10x more efficient!” It should be “So-and-so, someone you can relate to, has adopted this and look how much better their life has become; wouldn’t it be nice to be like them?”
This book reminds you of that. It can be distilled in one sentence: “The diffusion of technology is a SOCIAL process”

item.title: One fun benefit of spending so much time with enterprises is you get to see the array of AI implementation strategies that exist in companies right now. Unlike the early innings of cloud where there were really only a couple deployment patterns available -including being limited by only a couple i...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
One fun benefit of spending so much time with enterprises is you get to see the array of AI implementation strategies that exist in companies right now.
Unlike the early innings of cloud where there were really only a couple deployment patterns available -including being limited by only a couple infra vendors existing- AI actually has a much wider range of approaches in the enterprise.
If you ask 10 IT leaders what their coding agent strategy looks like, you get at least 5 different answers. If you ask about their end-user productivity agents, some have standardized on ChatGPT or Claude, others offer a choice of multiple solutions, and many have built their own orchestration layers for employees to use any model.
For models, we know the big ones, but increasingly enterprises are experimenting with OSS models, or are at least immensely curious about OSS and would jump at the right offering that felt safe. And increasingly there’s a set of vertical models and agents that equally show up in enterprises for a range of tailored use-cases.
For accessing data, some enterprises just have agents take on the role of the user, and others are setting up agent users that have their own identities. Some companies are setting up substantial guardrails on what agents can do, and others are putting responsibility on the user.
Given this heterogeneity this early on at the start, it means we’re in for years of landscape changes. Anyone who’s predicting ultimate market outcomes already probably will be wrong as nothing has formally settled in yet. Lots of opportunity ahead.

Every dollar earns until the moment you spend it. Why is this hard? Prediction under asym...
item.description:
作者：Aditya Agarwal 账号：@adityaag 简介：General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early Eng @facebook, CTO @Dropbox, Board @Flipkart | Optimist, Builder, Dad
.@TryRivo is building self-driving finance.
Agents connect to the checking account you already have, learn your cash flow, sweep dollars into Treasury-backed yield, and bring them back before your bills hit.
Every dollar earns until the moment you spend it.
Why is this hard? Prediction under asymmetric cost.
Money returned a day early costs you a little yield.
Money returned a day late bounces a bill and destroys trust.
@AmbrishTweets is one of the few people who has shipped this class of system before.
PhD in AI, 7,000+ citations, built consumer AI at Amazon, and led the L4 autonomy work at Cruise that launched robotaxis, before he came through @spc as a Founder Fellow.
Self-driving cars took two decades because the last edge cases were the hard ones.
Self-driving money is the same problem with a friendlier failure mode, and the founder building it has already solved the harder version once.

item.title: The best model for early product validation is almost never the best model for production. Talked to a bunch of founders this weekend. There’s a standard playbook emerging : 1/ Prototype with the best frontier models. Max quality. Ignore cost and latency. Learn what users actually want and iterate...
item.description:
作者：Madhu Guru 账号：@realmadhuguru 简介：Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.
The best model for early product validation is almost never the best model for production.
Talked to a bunch of founders this weekend. There’s a standard playbook emerging :
1/ Prototype with the best frontier models. Max quality. Ignore cost and latency. Learn what users actually want and iterate.
2/ Once the workflow and UX is validated, optimize like crazy for cost and latency - prompt eng, model routing, harnesses, smaller models, fine tuning.
I see most teams get stuck in step 1.

item.title: Chai Discovery's Bitter Lesson: Drug Design Is Another Scaling Problem
item.description:
播客：Training Data
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:22 One of our big guiding principles is just simplicity. So, like, when you look at a model like, let's say, CHI one, I think there are 23 distinct submodules in CHI one. And, like, when you're trying to iterate on something like that, it gets really hard because you're like, I kinda I need to understand each of these sub modules independently. I need to understand all of their behaviors, their dynamics, and, like, that doesn't actually scale that well. So, like, you can start to think, okay.
Speaker 1 | 00:22 - 00:31 How do I simplify this? How do I identify, like, what's what's really important? Once you have that, the whole research process and identifying these types of scaling directions becomes a lot simpler.
Speaker 2 | 00:48 - 01:01 We're here with Josh and Matt, two of the co founders of CHI Discovery. CHI is engineering molecules with AI. So it's something of a foundation model lab for biology. Sounds like a big idea, but let
Speaker 3 | 01:01 - 01:25 me just start there. What is the big idea? Thanks for having us on the show. One of the exciting things we're trying to do at CHI is to make the drug discovery process look a little bit more like engineering, and we've seen all the work happening with the LMs for cogeneration, for instance, right, and that works really well because code's a very simple obstruction, right, of like to kind of get across what you want to do. Biology doesn't look like that today.
Speaker 3 | 01:25 - 01:52 It's a lot of like trial and error. I think if we go back to the early days of just like modern biotech, right, a lot of the medicines that we have today were kind of discovered quite randomly. It was a bit serendipitous, and what we're trying to do is allow us to industrialize that process a little bit more and try to come up with the tools that we'd need in order to have abstraction layers, the same way we have that encoded in modern engineering, allows us to iterate really quickly and try to bring that, into biology and into drug discovery.
Speaker 2 | 01:52 - 02:15 So let me ask you a question on that then. So there's and tell me if this is a reasonable way to frame it. There's almost this boundary between that which can be engineered and that which needs to be tested in the real world. And it feels like that boundary has been moving over time. Like the proportion of the drug development process that can be engineered as opposed to trial and errored seems to be increasing.
Speaker 2 | 02:15 - 02:22 Is that a reasonable way to think about it? If so, can you talk about like what specific developments have pushed that boundary over time?
Speaker 3 | 02:22 - 02:41 I think that's one way to think about it. The way that we often, look at this is like the lab is an important part to verify that what you're doing is correct. And actually verification is a very big theme in AI as well. If you can evaluate that your model works, you can verify it, then you can start to hill climb that and you can make progress on it. So I think the lab is a very important part of this.
Speaker 3 | 02:41 - 03:03 And the question is how do we take drug discovery and make it look a lot more like drug design? So one of the reasons why we call this field drug discovery is we're often looking for a needle in a haystack. We'll screen millions, billions of molecules, try to find one that works. And if we can instead put in what is like the dream state of the molecule you want, and then the model can materialize that, that's going be really powerful. So it's not even a question of like reducing lab testing.
Speaker 3 | 03:03 - 03:24 I mean, maybe that happens as a result. I actually might even take the opposite side of the coin and we can talk about that where maybe we'd actually do even more lab testing because the ROI will increase the same way there's more software engineers, there's or more demand for software engineers now that they become more productive. There might be more demand for the lab. But I think the key part is how do we just change the paradigm here and how do we make it more design oriented?
Speaker 2 | 03:24 - 03:40 Can we talk about what is state of the art today? And then maybe let's take a little trip down memory lane. Five years ago, three years ago, one year ago, like what have been some of the major breakthroughs and like how has state of the art changed over the recent years?
Speaker 1 | 03:40 - 04:03 Yeah, I think the field has like, it's really evolved, especially like over the last decade. So it really wasn't until like, you can actually look back, there's like this biannual protein folding competition. So every two years, usually, a bunch of academic groups who compete in this protein folding competition. What would happen is, like, you kind of hold out these protein targets that no one's ever seen before. They never get deposited publicly.
Speaker 1 | 04:03 - 04:30 And then all these groups compete so you can predict the proteins the best. And, like, really, it wasn't until 2018 where you started to see this, like, big step change in in performance and then finally, again, in, like, 2020 with Alffold two. But, really, like, it was kind of like the advent of deep learning that really, like, kicked off this whole field. So at first, what you do, these are kind of like, bring me back to my original days in my adviser's lab. So we worked on, like, one of the first systems to do this with deep learning.
Speaker 1 | 04:30 - 05:04 What we would try to do is predict, like, the distances between amino acids and a protein, and then we'd have some render, which then took in, like, these kind of noisy and complete looking distances and then emitted some protein from that. And what's pretty remarkable is that with relatively minimal information, like, you could build a machine learning system that could actually produce something that really looks like a protein and, for the most part, was was correct. Like, there are still pretty big gaps. It didn't quite have the resolution of, like, what what we have today. Almost like with the early image generation models where it was, like, a little bit grainy, a little bit blurry, and now it's like, oh my gosh.
Speaker 1 | 05:04 - 05:24 Like, this is this is crazy high definition images, like, in seconds. So we kinda, like, saw that same evolution happen over time. So it started with protein folding. And then I guess once that became more realizable, there were kind of these other subproblems that people wanted to solve. So now given a protein structure, can I design, say, like a sequence which might fold to that?
Speaker 1 | 05:24 - 05:52 And that's getting closer and closer to, like, the drug design problem. So you're you're kind of, like, now thinking, okay, how do I start engineering proteins that match a certain shape or might perform a specific function? So people kind of studied that problem independently, and that was kind of like 2021, 2022 time. And then kind of these ideas began to merge together. It was really like the advent of diffusion models where we started to be able to like, okay, I can now generate a protein structure in a sequence kind of simultaneously.
Speaker 1 | 05:52 - 06:04 And I can start making these, like, what we would call prompts more and more realistic. So I can now prompt these models on a target that might have a certain shape and I can say, hey, wanna bind over here, kind of like add more real world constraints on the problem.
Speaker 2 | 06:04 - 06:08 What did you guys see in 2024 that made you think that was the right time to start the company?
Speaker 3 | 06:09 - 06:51 There were a lot of discussions that went into it. I remember one of these, early discussions actually back in Matt's house when we were, you know, Matt was showing me some of these results on like antibody antigen, like structure prediction. Matt was just talking about protein folding, but for a long time people thought that protein foldi...
